summary: Specifies YANG modules for representing assurance graphs, which break a service into atomic subservices. It is the companion to the architecture in RFC 9417 and follows the NMDA.

plainLanguage.summary: A way to write down, in computer-friendly form, a family tree of parts that make a service work.

what is a subservice in service assurance
subtitle: A YANG data model that writes down a service as a graph of small, separately health-checked parts.

tldr.problem: To assure a network service, tools need a machine-readable, vendor-independent way to describe the service's parts, how they depend on each other, and how healthy each one is.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9418 defines the ietf-service-assurance YANG module, which models a service as subservices linked by dependencies, each with a health score and symptoms. Two more modules add device and interface subservices, and the design can be augmented with new types.
tldr.outcome: It gives SAIN agents, orchestrators and collectors a shared data format for configuring an assurance graph and exporting its health. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 9418 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2023, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It is the data model companion to the architecture in RFC 9417.

sections.title: Why a Data Model for Assurance
sections.content:
RFC 9417 describes an architecture called Service Assurance for Intent-based Networking (SAIN). RFC 9418 complements it by specifying the data model for the interfaces between the components. The modules are written in YANG and are meant to be machine readable, vendor independent, and augmentable, so that SAIN agents can support and expose new subservices to SAIN orchestrators and collectors.

The modules conform to the Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA) defined in RFC 8342.
sections.plainLanguage: A monitoring system needs a common language so that different tools can talk about the same service. This document is that language.

sections.title: The Three Modules and Their Use Cases
sections.content:
The main module, ietf-service-assurance, defines objects for assuring services by splitting them into subservices organized by dependencies. Together the subservices and dependencies form an assurance graph. The module serves two use cases: configuring the graph (which subservices to assure, and the dependencies between them) and assurance telemetry (exporting the graph with health statuses and symptoms for each node).

The SAIN collector, which aggregates the output of several SAIN agents into a global assurance graph, is also expected to export the module. In that case only the telemetry use case applies.

Two further modules augment the base: ietf-service-assurance-device adds the device subservice and ietf-service-assurance-interface adds the interface subservice. The appendices add vendor-specific, IP connectivity and IS-IS examples.
sections.plainLanguage: There is one main module for the tree itself, and small add-on modules for particular kinds of parts, like a device or a network port.

sections.title: Subservices, Dependencies and the Assurance Graph
sections.content:
A subservice is a feature or a subpart of the network system that a service instance depends on. Examples are a device (with symptoms such as "CPU overloaded" or "Out of RAM") and ip-connectivity between two IP addresses (with symptoms such as "No route available"). The base model itself defines only one subservice type, which represents a service instance and acts as the root of that instance's assurance graph. It is identified by two parameters, service and instance-name.

Each subservice is keyed by type and id, and carries a list of dependencies, which may be empty. Each subservice instance is expected to appear only once in the global graph even if several service instances depend on it. A dependency is either impacting, meaning it affects the health of the dependent, or informational, meaning it may explain problems but does not change health.

The assured-services container lists, per service instance, all descendant subservices, as a query optimization so that a client can fetch a whole graph in one query.

Example from the text: an interface depends on its device with an impacting dependency, because the interface goes down if the device does. A dependency on the ecmp-load subservice is only informational, since services can stay healthy when ECMP load distribution changes.
sections.plainLanguage: A service is like a school day that depends on the bus, the building and the teacher. Some things stop the day if they break, and others just help explain why it went badly.

sections.title: Health Scores, Symptoms and Maintenance
sections.content:
An agent is expected to produce a health-score for each subservice, normally between 0 and 100, with the special value -1 meaning no score could be computed. A score below 100 must be explained by at least one symptom. How the score relates to each symptom's health-score-weight is left to the implementor; the text only offers as an example summing the weights, subtracting from 100, and using 0 if the result is negative.

Each symptom has a symptom-id, an agent-id, an optional weight, a start-date-time and an optional stop-date-time (absent while the symptom is active). The agent-id MUST be unique among agents, and the symptom-id MUST be unique among the symptoms of an agent.

If the optional under-maintenance container is present on a subservice, it inhibits emission of symptoms for that subservice and the subservices that depend on it, and a contact MUST be given. The leaf assurance-graph-last-change is updated on structural changes only, not on changes of health score or symptoms. History of the graph structure is out of scope; a time-series database or similar storage must be used for that.
sections.plainLanguage: Each part gets a mark out of 100. If a part is not perfect, it has to say why, like a teacher writing a note on a report card. A sign saying 'being repaired' quiets the alarms.

sections.title: Rejecting Circular Dependencies
sections.content:
A status that depends on itself cannot be computed, so circular dependencies must not exist. Avoiding them is the job of the SAIN orchestrator, but the RFC states what a server must do when it receives such data: a server implementing ietf-service-assurance MUST check for dependency loops whenever the graph is modified, and a modification that creates a loop MUST be rejected.

The text explains why this is not a plain YANG constraint: it would need a graph traversal written in XPath, and even then merging two loop-free graphs can produce a loop, as RFC 9417 shows with an example.
sections.plainLanguage: If A waits for B and B waits for A, nobody ever finishes. The server has to say no to any change that makes such a circle.

sections.title: Defining New Subservice Types
sections.content:
New subservice types are added by writing a new module. For IETF modules the name should start with ietf-service-assurance-, the namespace with urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-service-assurance-, and the prefix with sain-. The module should define a new identity based on subservice-base, whose name ends in -type, and a container named parameters that augments the parameter choice, restricted to the new type.

The device module follows this pattern with a single device string parameter, naming the device to assure. The interface module takes two strings, device and interface, aligned with the ietf-interfaces model in RFC 8343, where the interface name is the only key needed on a given device. Vendors may define their own subservice types in their own namespace, or augment IETF ones; Appendix A gives an example.
sections.plainLanguage: The tree has labeled slots for new kinds of parts. To add a new kind, you follow the naming rules and say what details identify it.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The modules are designed to be accessed through NETCONF (RFC 6241) or RESTCONF (RFC 8040), with the Network Configuration Access Control Model (RFC 8341) restricting what users can do. The writable subtree /subservices/subservice is sensitive: changing it alters the graph, which can cause false positives (reporting a healthy service as broken) or false negatives (hiding real issues, with consequences such as SLA violation fees or disruption of emergency calls).

The readable subtrees /subservices/subservice, /agents/agent and /assured-services/assured-service can reveal network structure and customer services, so a customer given telemetry access should see only nodes for their own services.

IANA registered three URIs in the IETF XML Registry and three modules in the YANG Module Names registry. These modules are not maintained by IANA.
sections.plainLanguage: Whoever can edit the tree can make the alarms lie, so only trusted people should edit it. Customers should see only their own part of the tree.

cells: The status of the dependency directly impacts the status of the dependent.
Its symptoms may be of interest to the dependent, but its status has no impact on the dependent.
